**DENVER, Colorado —** Barack Obama accepted the Democratic presidential nomination Thursday night before a roaring crowd of more than 75,000 people at Invesco Field, delivering the most important speech of his political career and becoming the first Black nominee of a major U.S. political party.

Speaking on the final night of the 2008 Democratic National Convention, Obama sought to introduce himself to a national audience not just as a symbol of change, but as a candidate ready to lead a country facing economic anxiety, war overseas and deep political division at home.

“With profound gratitude and great humility, I accept your nomination for the presidency of the United States,” Obama told the crowd, drawing thunderous applause inside the stadium.

The setting was unlike any previous convention finale. Instead of delivering his acceptance speech inside the convention hall, Obama’s campaign moved the event to the Denver Broncos’ football stadium, allowing tens of thousands of supporters to attend. The massive crowd waved American flags and campaign signs as Obama laid out his vision for the fall campaign against Republican Sen. John McCain.

Obama used the speech to argue that the election represented a clear choice between continuing the policies of President George W. Bush and pursuing a new direction on the economy, health care, energy and national security.

“America, we are better than these last eight years,” Obama said. “We are a better country than this.”

The Illinois senator directly criticized McCain, saying the Arizona Republican had voted too often with Bush and did not grasp the struggles of working families. But Obama also praised McCain’s military service, an effort to draw a distinction between personal respect and political disagreement.

“The record’s clear: John McCain has voted with George Bush 90 percent of the time,” Obama said. “I don’t know about you, but I’m not ready to take a 10 percent chance on change.”

Obama’s speech came 45 years to the day after Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his “I Have a Dream” address in Washington, a historical parallel that added weight to the evening. While Obama did not dwell on race, the significance of the moment was unmistakable for many delegates and supporters.

Throughout the week, Democrats worked to project unity after a long and bruising primary battle between Obama and Sen. Hillary Clinton. Clinton delivered a forceful endorsement earlier in the convention, urging her supporters to back Obama in November. Former President Bill Clinton also offered his support, telling Democrats that Obama was “ready to lead.”

Obama’s address focused heavily on the economy, promising tax relief for middle-class families, an end to tax breaks for companies that ship jobs overseas, expanded health care access, investment in renewable energy and a responsible end to the war in Iraq.

He also sought to counter Republican arguments that he lacked experience, framing judgment and temperament as central qualifications for the presidency.

“I will restore our moral standing, so that America is once again that last, best hope for all who are called to the cause of freedom,” Obama said.

The convention finale capped a rapid political rise for Obama, who was a state senator in Illinois just four years earlier when he delivered the keynote address at the 2004 Democratic National Convention in Boston. That speech launched him onto the national stage; Thursday night’s address placed him at the head of the Democratic Party.

The atmosphere inside Invesco Field was part political rally, part historic celebration. Supporters arrived hours before Obama took the stage, many wearing campaign T-shirts and buttons bearing his “Change” and “Hope” slogans. Fireworks erupted after the speech as Obama was joined onstage by his wife, Michelle, their daughters and running mate Sen. Joe Biden and his family.

Biden, introduced earlier in the week as Obama’s vice presidential pick, is expected to help the ticket appeal to working-class voters and bring decades of foreign policy experience to the campaign.

Republicans, preparing for their own convention the following week, dismissed the speech as lofty rhetoric short on specifics. McCain’s campaign argued that Obama was offering higher taxes and traditional liberal policies under the banner of change.

But for Democrats gathered in Denver, the night marked a turning point — the official launch of the general election campaign and a moment many described as historic.

Obama now heads into the final stretch of the presidential race facing a difficult challenge: converting the energy of his candidacy into votes in key battleground states. The campaign will focus heavily on states such as Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Florida, Virginia and Colorado, where economic concerns and turnout could determine the outcome.

Standing before one of the largest convention audiences in modern political history, Obama closed with an appeal to national purpose and civic responsibility.

“This election has never been about me,” he said. “It’s about you.”

With that, Democrats left Denver unified behind a nominee who promised change — and prepared for a hard-fought race to the White House.

The logistical challenge was enormous. Hosting a political acceptance speech in an open-air stadium required far more coordination than a typical convention hall event. Security was tight throughout the day, with the U.S. Secret Service working alongside Denver police, federal agencies, convention officials, stadium personnel, and campaign staff. Attendees passed through screening checkpoints before entering, and security perimeters reshaped movement around the stadium.

Inside, the operation was equally complex. Volunteers directed crowds through concourses, ushers handled seating, medical teams stood ready, and media organizations broadcast live from designated platforms. The stadium had to function simultaneously as a campaign stage, a television studio, a security zone, and a public gathering space for a massive audience.

The crowd itself reflected the broad coalition Obama’s campaign had worked to project: young and old, Black, white, Latino, Asian American, Native American, union members, military families, suburban parents, longtime Democrats, independents, and voters new to the political process. For those on the field, the event had the feel of a mass rally fused with a solemn political milestone. The night’s scale was deliberate: the campaign sought to show not only party unity but also public enthusiasm that extended beyond the walls of the convention itself.

“It doesn’t feel like a normal political speech,” said a young volunteer from Illinois. “It feels like the whole country is in this stadium.”

Outside, the city continued to manage the aftereffects of the event. As the speech concluded, crowds poured out into the streets, creating another wave of congestion. Trains, buses, sidewalks, and roadways filled with people leaving the stadium, many still chanting, talking, or quietly absorbing what they had witnessed.

CNN’s iReport has been flooded with videos from people inside and outside the stadium: supporters filming the long lines, the cheering crowds, the music, and the moment they first walk into the stadium and see the stage.

We’ve been in line for almost three hours, but nobody’s complaining. Everybody’s excited. You can hear people chanting from blocks away. It feels like we’re part of something bigger than just a speech.

**CNN iREPORT VIDEO — INSIDE INVESCO FIELD:**

**Obama Accepts Democratic Nomination Before Vast Denver Crowd on Historic Anniversary**

**By [Your Name], with reporting contributions from [Contributor 1] in Denver and [Contributor 2] in Washington**  
**DENVER, Aug. 28, 2008**

Barack Obama accepted the Democratic nomination for president Thursday night before a roaring crowd at Invesco Field at Mile High, becoming the first Black major-party nominee for the White House and tying his campaign’s promise of change to one of the most powerful anniversaries in American political history.

Speaking 45 years to the day after the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, Obama told an audience of more than 80,000 people that the nation stood at a defining moment.

“America, we are better than these last eight years,” Obama declared, drawing sustained applause from a stadium packed with delegates, volunteers, veterans, union members, students and families who had waited for hours under a clear Colorado sky. “We are a better country than this.”

The setting was unlike any previous convention finale. Instead of remaining inside the Pepsi Center, where Democrats had gathered for the first three nights of their convention, the Obama campaign moved the final session to the home of the Denver Broncos, transforming the football stadium into a vast outdoor arena of banners, flags and floodlights. Supporters waved blue “Change” signs and American flags while music echoed through the stands. Many wore campaign buttons bearing Obama’s face; others carried signs honoring King and the civil rights movement.

The symbolism of the night was impossible to miss. Obama did not present himself as the fulfillment of King’s dream, but he spoke directly to the long struggle for equal rights and the unfinished work of American democracy. The date connected the Illinois senator’s rise to the civil rights era, while the crowd — racially diverse, multi-generational and exuberant — offered a vivid image of the coalition Democrats hope will carry them to victory in November.

Obama paid tribute to those who “marched and struggled and bled” so that future generations might have broader opportunities, but he quickly pivoted to the economic anxieties facing voters in 2008: job losses, mortgage foreclosures, rising health-care costs, the war in Iraq and dependence on foreign oil.

“The promise of America has been threatened once more,” he said, framing the election as a choice between continuing President George W. Bush’s policies and turning toward what he called a new era of responsibility.

Obama sharply criticized Republican nominee-in-waiting John McCain, praising his military service but arguing that the Arizona senator had aligned himself too closely with the Bush administration. “John McCain has voted with George Bush 90 percent of the time,” Obama said. “I don’t know about you, but I’m not ready to take a 10 percent chance on change.”

The line brought one of the evening’s loudest responses, with the crowd rising in sections across the stadium.

The speech capped a carefully choreographed final night of the Democratic National Convention, designed both to celebrate history and to introduce Obama to voters still uncertain about his experience, ideology and readiness to lead. The program featured an array of Democratic officials, civil rights figures, military voices and ordinary Americans telling stories of economic hardship.

Former Vice President Al Gore, the party’s 2000 nominee and now a Nobel Peace Prize winner for his work on climate change, delivered one of the night’s most forceful addresses, warning that the country could not afford another administration that ignored environmental and energy challenges. Gore cast Obama as the candidate best prepared to confront global warming, rebuild alliances abroad and restore American credibility.

“Take it from me,” Gore told the crowd, alluding to the disputed 2000 election. “If you think the next appointments to the Supreme Court are important, you know that elections matter.”

New Mexico Gov. Bill Richardson, who had sought the Democratic nomination earlier in the campaign before endorsing Obama, also spoke, emphasizing foreign policy and the need for a president who could repair the United States’ standing in the world. Other speakers highlighted veterans’ issues, health care, education and the economic pressures on middle-class families.

Civil rights leaders and members of King’s family were present for the anniversary, adding solemnity to a night otherwise marked by the energy of a mass rally. Rep. John Lewis of Georgia, who spoke at the 1963 March on Washington and later became one of Congress’s most revered civil rights figures, was among those whose presence underscored the connection between the movement King helped lead and Obama’s barrier-breaking nomination.

The convention also included appearances and performances intended to broaden the evening’s appeal beyond traditional political speeches. Music filled long stretches of the program, with performers helping maintain the crowd’s energy as the stadium filled through the afternoon and early evening. Delegates in state sections mingled with campaign volunteers and first-time attendees, many of whom had received tickets through local Democratic organizations or the Obama campaign’s outreach operation.

As dusk settled over Denver, the stadium became a sea of camera flashes and waving signs. Chants of “Yes we can!” rolled through the stands before Obama appeared. When he walked onto the stage, joined by his wife, Michelle Obama, and their daughters after the speech, the moment had the atmosphere of both a political milestone and a national spectacle.

Michelle Obama, who had delivered a warmly received address earlier in the week, watched from the audience as her husband formally claimed the nomination. Sen. Joe Biden of Delaware, chosen days earlier as Obama’s running mate, had accepted the vice-presidential nomination the previous night, presenting himself as an experienced foreign policy hand and a champion of working-class Americans.

Obama’s task Thursday was larger: to reassure voters about his judgment, define his governing agenda and answer Republican criticism that his campaign offered inspiration without substance. His speech mixed biography, policy and attack. He invoked his Kansas grandparents, his mother, his work as a community organizer in Chicago and his belief that government should help create conditions for individual success.

He called for tax cuts for the middle class, an end to tax breaks for companies that ship jobs overseas, expanded health coverage, investment in renewable energy, better pay for teachers and a responsible end to the war in Iraq. He also stressed personal responsibility, telling parents to turn off televisions, help children with homework and take a more active role in their education.

“What is required is a new kind of politics,” Obama said, “one that can move beyond the stale arguments and bitter divisions of the past.”

Republicans, preparing for their own convention the following week in St. Paul, Minnesota, dismissed the event as political theater and argued that Obama remained untested. McCain’s campaign released a congratulatory advertisement marking Obama’s nomination and the King anniversary, but the general election battle was already sharpening around questions of experience, national security and the economy.

Still, for Democrats in Denver, Thursday night was a moment of confidence after a long and bruising primary fight between Obama and Sen. Hillary Rodham Clinton. Earlier in the week, Clinton had urged her supporters to unite behind Obama, and former President Bill Clinton followed with his own endorsement, praising Obama’s intelligence and temperament. By the time the convention moved to Invesco Field, party leaders were eager to show unity before a national television audience.

The crowd reflected that goal. Some attendees wore Hillary Clinton buttons alongside Obama stickers. Others carried signs reading “Unity” and “America’s Future.” Delegates hugged, danced in aisles and took photographs of the stadium bowl as it filled to capacity. Campaign aides said the outdoor venue allowed thousands of ordinary supporters — not only delegates and party insiders — to witness the acceptance speech in person.

For many in attendance, the anniversary of King’s speech gave the night its emotional weight.

“I never thought I would see this in my lifetime,” said one attendee, an older Black woman from Illinois who said she had followed Obama since his early political career. Nearby, younger voters described Obama less in terms of history than generational change, saying they were drawn by his opposition to the Iraq war and his call for a different political tone.

Obama ended his speech by returning to the theme of the American promise, urging voters to see the election as a test of national purpose.

“This is our chance to answer that call,” he said. “This is our moment. This is our time.”

Fireworks burst above the stadium after he finished, and red, white and blue confetti scattered across the stage as Obama, Biden and their families waved to the crowd. The cheers continued long after the speech ended, echoing through the open-air stadium on a night Democrats hoped would be remembered not only for its symbolism, but as the formal beginning of a winning fall campaign.
